sections.heading: What is OOP?
content: **Object-Oriented Programming (OOP)** is a way of structuring code around real-world 'things' called **objects** instead of just a sequence of instructions. Every object has **attributes** (data it holds) and **methods** (actions it can perform).

A **class** is a blueprint for creating objects. It defines what attributes and methods every object built from it will have. An **object** (or **instance**) is one specific thing created from that blueprint.
Real-world analogy: `Car` might be the class (the blueprint every car has a color, a speed, and can accelerate). `my_car = Car("red")` is one specific object built from that blueprint.

sections.heading: Defining a Class
content: You define a class with the `class` keyword, using **PascalCase** naming (capitalized, no underscores) to distinguish it from variables and functions: `class Rocket:`.
This is the structure the **Rocket Class** exercise is built on a class representing a rocket with attributes like `name` and `fuel`, ready to have methods added for launching, refueling, and so on.

sections.heading: __init__ and self
content: `__init__` is a special method Python calls **automatically** every time you create a new object from the class. It's used to set up (initialize) the object's starting attributes.

`self` refers to **the specific object being created or used** it's how a method accesses that object's own attributes. It's always the first parameter in every method inside a class, and Python passes it automatically you never type it in when calling the method.

`self.name = name` means: take the `name` value passed in, and store it on **this particular object** as an attribute called `name`. Every object gets its own separate copy `rocket1.name` and `rocket2.name` can hold completely different values.

sections.heading: Methods & Attributes
content: An **attribute** is a piece of data stored on an object (`self.fuel`). A **method** is a function defined inside a class that an object can perform, always taking `self` as its first parameter so it can access that object's own data.

You call a method on a specific object using dot notation: `rocket1.launch()`. This is exactly the pattern behind the **Bank Account** exercise methods like `deposit(amount)` and `withdraw(amount)` that read and update `self.balance`, keeping each account's balance isolated from every other account object.

sections.heading: Bringing It Together
content: The **Space Explorer Character** exercise ties the whole station together: a class representing a playable character with attributes (`health`, `name`, `inventory`) and methods that change those attributes over time (`take_damage()`, `heal()`, `pick_up_item()`).

This is also a great mental bridge back to your **Checkpoint 01 (Space Adventure)** project the same game logic you built with plain variables and `if`/`while` can now be rebuilt more cleanly using a class, where the character's state lives neatly inside one object instead of scattered loose variables.
